title: Rules Rail
description: Run a number through the rules that need no columns, and find the one thing subtraction will not let you do.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find out which things you are allowed to do to a subtraction, and the one thing that addition allows and this does not.
writeup.look: A rail with a number card riding on it, rule cards waiting underneath, and a two lane order gate standing at its left hand end.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rules Rail' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rule cards run against the rule cards this phase has laid out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each card leaves the rail and the second fixed at the number of cards waiting. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The order gate stands at the left of the working area, 300 by 300 at 64,202: two lanes 300 by 138 one above the other, each with a mouth at its left, a throat, and an opening at its right where an answer comes out. The same pair of numbers is loaded into both lanes, the greater one leading in the upper lane and the smaller one leading in the lower, and both lanes run together on one press. The upper lane carries its pair through and sets an answer down at its opening; the lower lane runs in step until it reaches a column with less in it than is being asked for, and there it simply stops, with the pair left standing in the throat, nothing marked and no red anywhere. The swap control sits under the gate at 64,516, 300 by 76: pressed while a jam is still showing, it loads the identical pair into both lanes as an addition instead, both lanes run to the end, and the two totals land at their openings on the same tick, so the rule that holds and the rule that does not are read side by side without either being announced. The rail runs across the rest of the working area, 720 by 8 at 394,320, carrying one number card 300 by 104 that rides along it. The place chart slides in behind the number, 720 by 150 at 394,232, one named place above each digit and read out from the right hand end. The six rule cards lie beneath the rail in two rows of three, each 168 by 84 with 12 between them, the upper row at 394,400 reading take nothing, take one and take the number itself, the lower row at 394,496 reading take ten, take a hundred and take a thousand. A card dragged on to the rail acts in one movement while the place it names lights in the chart, and hold the rest draws every other digit pinned in place for as long as the movement lasts. Take one steps the whole card back to the number just before it, with the rollover drawn at the digit where it happens; take nothing moves nothing at all and the card is read out afterwards as the same number it arrived as; take the number itself empties the card and leaves it standing blank. The fact bay runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 120 at 64,586, holding three number cards and three lines: the addition fact along the top and two empty subtraction lines under it, both of which have to begin from the total card. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an answer is asked for, and beside them a word pad carrying the five terms the chapter closes on, minuend, subtrahend, difference, rounding and estimate, turned towards a partner for the quiz and answered by press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number standing on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a column that has lent is told by the single strike through its digit and by the smaller value written small above it. No lane of the order gate is ever marked wrong and no jam is ever drawn in red: a lane that stops has simply run out of things to take, and that is a fact about the numbers rather than a mistake the child made.
writeup.finish: The card shows the rail with the last rule that ran still lit, and the order gate holding the pair that jammed.

phases.win: one lane jams for want of enough to take, and both addition lanes land together
phases.does: runs both lanes, watches one jam, then loads the pair as an addition
phases.goal: the greater number has to go first, unlike two numbers being added
phases.says: Swap them over. Does subtraction let you? Did adding let you?
phases.check: In an addition you may write the two numbers in either order. Write down what happens if you try that in a subtraction.
phases.feels: one of the two lanes simply has nothing left in it to take from
phases.hands: On squared paper write eighteen take ten and work it. Then write ten take eighteen underneath and try to work it column by column out loud, without being rescued. Then write the same two numbers as an addition, once each way round, and put the two totals side by side. Ask which of the two workings let the numbers be swapped and which one did not.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is leading in the lane that stopped? Second rung, the phase's: can more be taken out of a number than the number holds? Third rung: the gate is cut to a single column pair and the child sends it through both ways. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the chapter before this one taught that two numbers being added may be written in either order and the total does not change, and nothing in the way a subtraction is written says the rule has stopped.
wrong.move: swaps the two numbers over so that the subtraction reads the easier way round, because addition allowed exactly that.
wrong.screen: the swapped pair is sent through the gate as it stands and the lane jams at the first column with less in it than is being asked for, with the pair left standing and nothing marked. The swap control then loads the identical two numbers as an addition, both lanes run to the end and their totals land together, and the two runs are left on the stage one above the other so that the rule that holds and the rule that does not can be read side by side.

wrong.why: a column turned round quietly gives an answer where there was not one to be had, and a lane that reaches its opening looks like a lane that worked.
wrong.move: keeps the smaller number in front and takes the smaller digit from the greater one in each column, so that the lane runs after all.
wrong.screen: the lane is run again at walking pace with each column read out in the order it is written, the leading number's digit named first, and every column the child turned round is ringed amber and read again as it stands. The same pair is then run the proper way round in the lane above, and the two answers stand at their openings together with the check by addition run on each of them.

phases.screen: the order gate with the same pair loaded into both of its lanes
phases.soWhat: The greater number goes first in a subtraction and the two cannot be swapped, though the two numbers in an addition can.

phases.win: the card stands unchanged, steps back one, and empties, in that order
phases.does: drops each of the three in turn and says what moved before it moves
phases.goal: three rules that need no columns at all
phases.says: Take nothing. Take one. Take the whole thing. Say each answer before you drop it.
phases.check: Away from the screen: what is left when a number has nothing taken from it, and what is left when it has the whole of itself taken from it?
phases.feels: three answers, and not one column worked between them
phases.hands: Write 62,904 three times down a sheet of squared paper and take nothing from the first, one from the second and the whole number from the third. Insist that each answer is said out loud before it is written, and that nothing is set out in columns. Then ask which of the three answers would change if the number had been six digits long instead.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how much was actually taken off the card? Second rung, the phase's: if nothing left the card, what can be standing on it? Third rung: the rail is cut to a two digit number and all three cards are run on it in turn. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: taking nothing away and taking the whole number away are met one after the other, and the word nothing turns up in both of them.
wrong.move: writes nothing at all as the answer when nothing has been taken away, because the two rules were learnt in the same breath.
wrong.screen: the nothing card runs again at walking pace with the place chart behind the number and every digit pinned, and not one of them moves; the card that leaves the rail is read out place by place as the same number it arrived as. The itself card is then run on a second card beside it and that one empties, and the two cards are left standing together for comparison.

wrong.why: one more and one less are the same small step in opposite directions, and the number that comes next is the one said aloud far more often.
wrong.move: steps the card forward to the number just after instead of back to the number just before.
wrong.screen: a short strip of the numbers either side of the card is drawn under the rail with the card sitting on its own place, and the step is animated along it; the number just before lights and the number just after is left plain. The child's answer stays on the strip exactly where it was put, one place past the card, and both stay showing.

phases.screen: a number on the rail with the nothing, one and itself cards waiting
phases.soWhat: Taking nothing leaves a number alone, taking one steps it back to the number just before it, and taking a number from itself empties it.
phases.concept: One, nothing, and the number itself

phases.win: the named digit drops by one, the rest stay pinned and the chart agrees
phases.does: names the digit that will drop, then drops the card and checks
phases.goal: a round amount drops the digit of its own place and no other
phases.says: Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you drop the card.
phases.check: Take a thousand away from a six digit number of your own. Which digit changed, and how did you find it?
phases.feels: one digit moves and none of the others cares
phases.hands: Write 58,271 on squared paper and take ten from it, then a hundred, then a thousand, each from the original number. Ring the digit that changed each time and check that every other digit was copied down untouched. Then do the same three on 4,37,912 and ask whether the ringed digit sits in the same position along the number as it did before.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which place does this card name? Second rung, the phase's: which end of the number do you count the places from? Third rung: the chart is cut to three places with a three digit number on the rail and the child runs the ten card and the hundred card on it. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left, and on a five digit number counting from either end can land on the same digit, which is often enough for the habit to survive unnoticed.
wrong.move: counts the places from the left hand end of the number, so the digit that drops is the wrong one.
wrong.screen: the place chart slides in behind the number and is read out from the right hand end, with the place the card names lit the whole way. The digit the child dropped keeps its own mark where it was put, and the same rule card is then run on 4,37,912, where 4,36,912 and 4,27,912 stand one under the other and the two ways of counting plainly part.

wrong.why: every change to a number so far has meant a column being worked and something moving next door, and a digit standing perfectly still while its neighbour drops looks unfinished.
wrong.move: drops the named digit and nudges the digits beside it as well, as though the whole number had to shift along.
wrong.screen: hold the rest pins every other digit and the card is run again with each pinned digit drawn holding its place as the movement passes it. The number is then read out place by place before and after, the two readings standing one under the other, and only the single named place differs between them.

phases.screen: the rail with the place chart behind the number and every digit pinned
phases.soWhat: Taking ten drops the tens digit, taking a hundred drops the hundreds digit and taking a thousand drops the thousands digit, and nothing else moves.
phases.concept: Ten, a hundred and a thousand each touch one digit

phases.win: both subtraction facts stand under the addition, built from the same three cards
phases.does: turns the fact over and writes both subtraction facts from the same cards
phases.goal: one addition fact turns over into two subtraction facts
phases.says: Three cards, and you have written one fact. How many more are hiding in them?
phases.check: You are given two numbers and the total they make. How many subtraction facts can you write from them, and which number does each one begin at?
phases.feels: three cards, and every one of the three facts uses all three of them
phases.hands: Write 32,140 + 45,209 = 77,349 on a strip of paper and cut the strip into three number cards. Ask for every true line that can be made from those three cards and no others, and have each one written out. Then ask which card every subtraction line had to begin from, and why that is so.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the three cards is the total? Second rung, the phase's: if one part is taken off the total, which card is left? Third rung: the bay is cut to a two digit addition fact and the child writes both subtraction lines from it. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the three cards can be laid out in more ways than three, and a subtraction using two of them looks like it belongs to the same family as the others.
wrong.move: writes a subtraction that takes one of the two parts away from the other part.
wrong.screen: the three cards are read again as two parts and a total with the total card lit, and the child's line is worked anyway in the lane beside it, landing on 13,069, which is not written on any of the three cards. Both lines stay on the stage, with the lines that begin from the total lit and the one that does not left plain.

wrong.why: turning the addition over once has already produced something new, and one new fact feels like a complete answer to the question that was asked.
wrong.move: writes one subtraction fact and reports the fact bay finished.
wrong.screen: the fact bay keeps the line the child wrote and lifts the part card that line took away, leaving the other part standing on its own and unused; the bay then asks for a line that begins at the total and ends on that card, and both subtraction facts finish standing under the addition, all three built from the same three cards.

phases.screen: the fact bay holding one addition fact on three cards
phases.soWhat: Two numbers and their total hold one addition fact and two subtraction facts.
phases.concept: Every addition fact holds two subtraction facts

writeup.delight: The first phase, at the order gate. The same pair is sent into both lanes on one press and they run in step, column for column, until the lower lane arrives at a column with less in it than is being asked for and simply comes to a halt, with the pair still standing in the throat and nothing marked anywhere. Press the swap control while that jam is still sitting on the stage and the identical two numbers are loaded as an addition: both lanes run all the way through this time, and their two totals land at the openings on the very same tick. The jam and the pair of matching totals are left on the stage together, and the voice says nothing about either.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the order gate stands at the left with the same pair of numbers already loaded into both of its lanes, the greater one leading in the upper lane and the smaller one leading in the lower, and both mouths closed. On the second a number card rides the middle of the rail with three rule cards waiting under it, one reading take nothing, one take one and one take the number itself. On the third the place chart has already slid in behind the number and every digit is pinned, with the three round amount cards lying below. On the fourth the fact bay holds one addition fact on three cards and two empty lines beneath it. The running count at the top left holds the rule cards run against the rule cards waiting, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the closed mouth of the lower lane, or the nothing card, or the digit the next card will act on, or the total card in the fact bay, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what is going to happen before anything is dropped. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number on the rail, any rule card, with the order gate open and the fact bay loaded alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on order, on nothing and one and the number itself, on which digit a round amount touches, and on turning an addition fact over.
voiceLines: A number rides the rail. Say what a rule card will do to it before you drop the card.
Swap them over. Does subtraction let you? Did adding let you?
Take nothing. Take one. Take the whole thing. Say each answer before you drop it.
Which digit is going to move this time? Say it before you drop the card.
Three cards, and you have written one fact. How many more are hiding in them?
Another number on the rail. Which digit is going to move this time?
Free play. Any number, any rule card, the order gate open and the fact bay loaded.
Send that card again at walking pace and watch the place chart behind the number.
Every rule run without a column being worked, and one thing subtraction would not let you do.

observations.why: The lane led by the smaller number reaches a column with less in it than is being asked for.
observations.soWhat: The two numbers in a subtraction cannot be swapped, and the greater one has to go first.
observations.observe: The same pair ran into both lanes together and only one of the two lanes came out with an answer.

observations.why: Adding puts two amounts together, and it makes no difference which of them is counted on to the other.
observations.soWhat: The order rule from the chapter before is still true; it is simply not this chapter's rule.
observations.observe: Loaded as an addition, that very same pair ran in both lanes and the two totals landed together.

observations.why: Ten, a hundred and a thousand are each worth exactly one of the place they name.
observations.soWhat: A round amount is taken off a number by sight, without anything being set out in columns.
observations.observe: Taking a round amount moved one digit and left every other digit standing exactly where it was.

observations.why: Two parts and a total are one relationship, and it can be written from the total as well as towards it.
observations.soWhat: Knowing an addition fact is already knowing two subtraction facts.
observations.observe: Three number cards produced three facts, and two of the three were subtractions.

phases.screen: the order gate with the same pair loaded into both of its lanes
phases.win: one lane jams for want of enough to take, and both addition lanes land together
phases.traceback: Both lanes run again at walking pace: the lane led by the smaller number stops with nothing left to take, then the same pair runs as an addition and both totals land together.
ladder: Which of the two numbers is leading in the lane that stopped?
In which lane is the greater number on top?
Which lane came out with an answer, and which number led it?
Can more be taken out of a number than the number holds?
Look at the lane that stopped. Is there enough in its first number to take the second away?

phases.screen: a number on the rail with the nothing, one and itself cards waiting
phases.win: the card stands unchanged, steps back one, and empties, in that order
phases.traceback: The card runs again at walking pace with the place chart behind it and every digit pinned; the step back or the emptying is drawn beside its partner card, and the card ends on the right number.
ladder: How much was actually taken off the card?
Did the card on the rail take nothing at all, or all of it?
Taking one left 38,469. Was the blank bigger or smaller than that?
If nothing left the card, what can be standing on it?
Say the number on the card, then say how much the card on the rail takes from it.

phases.screen: the rail with the place chart behind the number and every digit pinned
phases.win: the named digit drops by one, the rest stay pinned and the chart agrees
phases.traceback: The places are counted from the ones end with the named place lit; every other digit is pinned while that one drops, and the number before and after is read one under the other.
ladder: Which place does this card name?
Which digit of 52,836 is the tens digit, and which is the thousands?
Which place did the other child take the thousand from?
Which end of the number do you count the places from?
Count the places from the ones end. Ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.

phases.screen: the fact bay holding one addition fact on three cards
phases.win: both subtraction facts stand under the addition, built from the same three cards
phases.traceback: The three cards are read as two parts and a total with the total lit; the child's line is worked anyway, and both facts that begin from the total are written in full.
ladder: Which of the three cards is the total?
Which card did each of your lines start from?
Which number is the sum, and what is it taken from?
If one part is taken off the total, which card is left?
Start each line from the total, the greatest of the three cards.

gate.lanes: two lanes side by side, the greater number leading on the left; a lane runs its columns from the ones and stops when there is nothing left to take

bay.rows: the addition fact on three cards, two subtraction lines built from them

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Both lanes run again at walking pace: the lane led by the smaller number stops with nothing left to take, then the same pair runs as an addition and both totals land together.

Phase 2: The card runs again at walking pace with the place chart behind it and every digit pinned; the step back or the emptying is drawn beside its partner card, and the card ends on the right number.
Phase 3: The places are counted from the ones end with the named place lit; every other digit is pinned while that one drops, and the number before and after is read one under the other.
Phase 4: The three cards are read as two parts and a total with the total lit; the child's line is worked anyway, and both facts that begin from the total are written in full.

voice.opening: A number rides the rail. Say what a rule card will do to it before you drop the card.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every rule run without a column being worked, and one thing subtraction would not let you do.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: Take 24 from 61. Now try taking 61 from 24. Is it the same answer?

question.en: Take 24 from 61. Now try taking 61 from 24. Is it the same answer?

items.planAnswer: No. 61 - 24 = 37, but 61 cannot be taken from 24 at all

items.planQuestion: Does 92,415 - 30,207 give the same answer as 30,207 - 92,415?

question.en: Look at 92,415 − 30,207. Does 30,207 − 92,415 give the same?

items.planAnswer: No. The first gives 62,208, and the second cannot be worked, because the greater number has to go first

items.planQuestion: In addition you may swap the two numbers over. What is the rule in subtraction?

question.en: In addition you may swap the two numbers over. What is the rule in subtraction?

items.planAnswer: The two numbers cannot be swapped, and the greater one goes first

items.planQuestion: Write the answers to 45,208 - 0, then 45,208 - 1, then 45,208 - 45,208.

question.en: Write the answers. 45,208 − 0. Then 45,208 − 1. Then take 45,208 from itself.
Fill the blanks. 67,341 − 0. Then take 67,341 from itself.
Fill the blank. Which number, take away 1, leaves 38,469?

items.planQuestion: Take 100 from 74,536, then take 1000 from 74,536, and say which digit moved each time.

question.en: Take 100 from 74,536. Then take 1,000 from 74,536. Which digit moved each time?

items.planAnswer: 74,436 and 73,536. The hundreds digit dropped first, then the thousands digit

items.planQuestion: A child takes 1000 from 83,472 and writes 83,372. Is that right?

question.en: A child takes 1,000 from 83,472. The child writes 83,372. Is that right? Type what it should be.

items.planAnswer: No. It should be 82,472, because taking a thousand drops the thousands digit and not the hundreds digit

items.planQuestion: From the addition fact 41,203 + 26,150 = 67,353, write the two subtraction facts.

question.en: Here is an addition fact on three cards. Write the two subtraction facts it holds.

items.planQuestion: From 35,124 + 42,613 = 77,737, write the two subtraction facts.

question.en: Here is another addition fact. Which two subtraction facts are inside it?

items.planQuestion: Subtract the sum of 24,180 and 31,725 from 99,999.

question.en: Find the sum of 24,180 and 31,725. Then subtract it from 99,999.

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
